claim: Mated Drosophila melanogaster females increase sugar intake.
source: Here, we find that mated Drosophila melanogaster females increase sugar intake, which is regulated by the activity of sexually dimorphic insulin receptor (Lgr3) neurons.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-H.

claim: Increased sugar intake in mated females is regulated by the activity of sexually dimorphic Lgr3+ neurons.
source: Here, we find that mated Drosophila melanogaster females increase sugar intake, which is regulated by the activity of sexually dimorphic insulin receptor (Lgr3) neurons.
evidence: The abstract states this regulatory relationship, supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: In virgin females, Lgr3+ cells have reduced activity as they receive inhibitory input from active, female-specific pCd-2 cells.
source: In virgins, Lgr3+ cells have reduced activity as they receive inhibitory input from active, female-specific pCd-2 cells, restricting sugar intake.
evidence: The abstract states this mechanism, supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 6D-E showing inhibitory responses.

claim: During copulation, males deposit sex peptide into the female reproductive tract.
source: During copulation, males deposit sex peptide into the female reproductive tract, which silences a three-tier mating status circuit and initiates the female postmating response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Chen et al., 1988; Liu and Kubli, 2003) in the introduction.

claim: Sex peptide silences a three-tier mating status circuit and initiates the female postmating response.
source: During copulation, males deposit sex peptide into the female reproductive tract, which silences a three-tier mating status circuit and initiates the female postmating response.
evidence: The abstract states this, and it is supported by citations (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020) and experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: pCd-2 neurons become silenced after mating due to direct synaptic input from the mating status circuit.
source: We show that pCd-2 neurons also become silenced after mating due to the direct synaptic input from the mating status circuit.
evidence: The abstract states this, supported by connectomics data in Figure 5A and functional connectivity data in Figures 5G-H.

claim: In mated females, pCd-2 inhibition is attenuated, activating downstream Lgr3+ neurons and promoting sugar intake.
source: Thus, in mated females pCd-2 inhibition is attenuated, activating downstream Lgr3+ neurons and promoting sugar intake.
evidence: The abstract states this mechanism, supported by optogenetic manipulation data in Figures 5I-J and 6G.

claim: The mating circuit transforms the mated signal into a long-term hunger signal.
source: Together, this circuit transforms the mated signal into a long-term hunger signal.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mating circuit alters nutrient sensing centers to increase feeding in mated females.
source: Our results demonstrate that the mating circuit alters nutrient sensing centers to increase feeding in mated females, providing a mechanism to increase intake in anticipation of the energetic costs associated with reproduction.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement, supported by the experimental data showing connections to Lgr3+ neurons.

claim: Increased feeding in mated females provides a mechanism to increase intake in anticipation of the energetic costs associated with reproduction.
source: Our results demonstrate that the mating circuit alters nutrient sensing centers to increase feeding in mated females, providing a mechanism to increase intake in anticipation of the energetic costs associated with reproduction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the findings, supported by the observation that eggless females still show increased feeding (Figure 3A).

claim: Mated Drosophila females increase total food intake.
source: In Drosophila, mated females increase egg production while also escalating nutrient consumption. Observed diet-related changes include an increase in total food intake (Carvalho et al., 2006) and the development of appetites for protein and salt (Vargas et al., 2010; Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Carvalho et al., 2006.

claim: Mated Drosophila females develop appetites for protein and salt.
source: In Drosophila, mated females increase egg production while also escalating nutrient consumption. Observed diet-related changes include an increase in total food intake (Carvalho et al., 2006) and the development of appetites for protein and salt (Vargas et al., 2010; Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Vargas et al., 2010; Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Walker et al., 2015.

claim: Dietary protein and salt are likely processed and used during egg assembly.
source: These two nutrients have been linked to reproduction as dietary protein and salt are likely processed and used during egg assembly (Simpson et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Simpson et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2015.

claim: Sugar is the fly's main energy source.
source: Sugar is the fly's main energy source (Simpson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Simpson et al., 2015.

claim: Females use sugar during egg production when dietary carbohydrates are synthesized into lipids.
source: Females use sugar during egg production when dietary carbohydrates are synthesized into lipids (Brown et al., 2022) and packed into the developing ova (Sieber and Spradling, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Brown et al., 2022.

claim: Dietary carbohydrates are packed into the developing ova.
source: Females use sugar during egg production when dietary carbohydrates are synthesized into lipids (Brown et al., 2022) and packed into the developing ova (Sieber and Spradling, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Sieber and Spradling, 2015.

claim: Mated females increase their locomotor activity.
source: Mated females also increase their locomotor activity (Isaac et al., 2010), resulting in elevated metabolic rates (Brown et al., 2022) and driving the need for additional calories.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Isaac et al., 2010.

claim: Increased locomotor activity in mated females results in elevated metabolic rates.
source: Mated females also increase their locomotor activity (Isaac et al., 2010), resulting in elevated metabolic rates (Brown et al., 2022) and driving the need for additional calories.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Brown et al., 2022.

claim: Excessive sugar negatively impacts fly health.
source: However, as excessive sugar negatively impacts fly health (Baenas and Wagner, 2022), sugar intake must be tightly regulated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Baenas and Wagner, 2022.

claim: The sugar-to-protein ratio influences reproductive output and longevity.
source: Although the sugar-to-protein ratio influences reproductive output and longevity (Simpson et al., 2015), the absolute levels of sugar intake of mated females remain untested.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Simpson et al., 2015.

claim: Sex peptide is a 36-amino acid peptide produced in the male seminal fluid and transferred to females during copulation.
source: SP is a 36-amino acid peptide that is produced in the male seminal fluid and transferred to females during copulation (Chen et al., 1988; Liu and Kubli, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Chen et al., 1988; Liu and Kubli, 2003.

claim: Sex peptide binds to its receptor (SPR) which is expressed in sensory neurons in the uterus.
source: SP binds to its receptor (SPR; Yapici et al., 2008) which is expressed in sensory neurons (sex peptide sensory neurons, SPSNs) in the uterus (Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Yapici et al., 2008; Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009.

claim: SPSNs convey mating status to sex peptide abdominal ganglia (SAG) neurons that ascend to the central brain.
source: SPSNs convey mating status to sex peptide abdominal ganglia (SAG) neurons that ascend to the central brain (Feng et al., 2014) and synapse onto pC1 neurons (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Feng et al., 2014.

claim: SAG neurons synapse onto pC1 neurons.
source: SPSNs convey mating status to sex peptide abdominal ganglia (SAG) neurons that ascend to the central brain (Feng et al., 2014) and synapse onto pC1 neurons (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The SPSN-SAG-pC1 circuit is active in virgin females and silenced after mating.
source: This female-specific SPSN-SAG-pC1 circuit is active in virgin females and silenced after mating (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Reception of SP and silencing of the SPSN-SAG-pC1 circuit initiates the long-term postmating response.
source: Reception of SP and the consequential silencing of this circuit initiates the long-term postmating response, an umbrella term used to describe the shift in many behaviors after mating including reduced sexual receptivity and increased egg laying (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Different neurons downstream of pC1 independently adjust individual postmating behaviors.
source: Although the three-tier SPSN-SAG-pC1 circuit appears to coordinate postmating state (Walker et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020), different neurons downstream of pC1 independently adjust individual behaviors (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Reception of SP or artificial silencing of SPSNs and SAG neurons causes an increase in the consumption of both salt and protein.
source: The reception of SP during mating or the artificial silencing of the first-order SPSNs and second-order SAG neurons causes an increase in the consumption of both salt and protein (Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Walker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Walker et al., 2015.

claim: The 'borboleta' region modulates yeast-based feeding in mated females.
source: For example, with the use of whole brain imaging, researchers have identified the 'borboleta' region as a modulator of yeast-based feeding in mated females. However, if and how this region is regulated by the SPSNs, SAG, or pC1 remains unknown (Münch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Münch et al., 2022.

claim: 72 hr postmated females consumed sucrose for a significantly longer duration than virgins or 1 hr postmated females.
source: We found that 72 hr postmated females consumed for a significantly longer duration on sucrose solution than virgins or 1 hr postmated females (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Changes in sucrose consumption manifest 6–24 hr after copulation.
source: These studies demonstrate that mated females consume more sugar than virgins and that changes in sucrose consumption manifest 6–24 hr after copulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on data from Figure 1C.

claim: Mated females consume more sucrose by engaging in longer feeding times rather than by initiating more feeding events.
source: Thus, mated females consume more by engaging in longer feeding times rather than by initiating more feeding events.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on data from Figures 1E and 1F showing bout duration differences but not bout number differences.

claim: Mated females consume significantly more sucrose volume than virgins.
source: We directly tested this using a capillary feeder (CAFE; Ja et al., 2007; Figure 1G) and found that mated females consume significantly more sucrose than virgins (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Virgin and mated females have similar feeding initiation propensities.
source: To directly test this, we monitored proboscis extension upon sugar taste detection (Figure 1I) and found that virgin and mated females have similar feeding initiation propensities (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figures 1J and 1K.

claim: Hunger increases the sensitivity of gustatory neurons to sugar.
source: Hunger increases the sensitivity of gustatory neurons to sugar (Inagaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Inagaki et al., 2012.

claim: Gustatory sensitivity is not altered by mating.
source: Stimulation of the fly proboscis with sugar elicited similar responses in gustatory axons regardless of mating status (Figure 2B–D), demonstrating that gustatory sensitivity is not altered by mating and not likely to contribute to changes in feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 2B-D.

claim: Despite a lack of egg production, eggless mated females consumed more sucrose than eggless virgins.
source: We found that despite a lack of egg production (Walker et al., 2015; Ohlstein and McKearin, 1997; Mével-Ninio et al., 1996), mated females consumed more sucrose than virgins, demonstrating that the change in postmated sucrose feeding is not driven by egg production itself.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The change in postmated sucrose feeding is not driven by egg production itself.
source: We found that despite a lack of egg production (Walker et al., 2015; Ohlstein and McKearin, 1997; Mével-Ninio et al., 1996), mated females consumed more sucrose than virgins, demonstrating that the change in postmated sucrose feeding is not driven by egg production itself.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on experiments with eggless females shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sucrose feeding changes are anticipatory in nature and a consequence of a need-independent mechanism.
source: Instead, this result suggests that sucrose feeding changes are anticipatory in nature and a consequence of a need-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the eggless female experiments.

claim: Virgin females with SPSNs silenced consumed significantly more sucrose than virgin controls.
source: Virgin females with SPSNs silenced consumed significantly more sucrose than virgin controls (Figure 3D and E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–1F), recapitulating the mated phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figures 3D, 3E, and supplementary figures.

claim: Mated females increase sucrose consumption after mating via the SPSNs.
source: This data argues that mated females increase sucrose consumption after mating via the SPSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on SPSN silencing experiments.

claim: Acutely silencing SAGs significantly increased sucrose consumption.
source: Monitoring consumption over time, we found that acutely silencing SAGs significantly increased sucrose consumption (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Acutely silencing pC1 significantly increased sucrose consumption.
source: Downstream of SAG, we found that acutely silencing pC1 also significantly increased sucrose consumption (Figure 3H and I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–D), demonstrating that pC1 neurons regulate postmating sucrose feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figures 3H and 3I.

claim: The increased sugar consumption after mating is part of the repertoire of behavioral changes induced after copulation by SP acting on the SPSN-SAG-pC1 mating status circuit.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the increased sugar consumption after mating is part of the repertoire of behavioral changes induced after copulation by SP acting on the SPSN-SAG-pC1 mating status circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the circuit manipulation experiments.

claim: Manipulation of vpoDNs or oviDNs did not affect sucrose consumption.
source: We found no difference in sucrose consumption upon manipulation of vpoDNs or oviDNs (Figure 4B, C, F and G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neither the circuits for egg laying nor sexual receptivity mediate postmating sucrose feeding.
source: These studies argue that neither of the previously identified circuits responsible for a single postmating response, egg laying, and sexual receptivity, mediate postmating sucrose feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the vpoDN and oviDN manipulation experiments.

claim: Three pCd-2 neurons (pCd-2a, pCd-2b, and pCd-2c) are strongly connected to SAG (39 synapses) and pC1 (146 synapses).
source: This approach identified three pCd-2 neurons (Kimura et al., 2015; Nojima et al., 2021), pCd-2a, pCd-2b, and pCd-2c (Figure 5A), that are strongly connected to SAG (39 synapses) and pC1 (146 synapses).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by connectomics data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: pCd-2 cells have processes that descend into the prow region of the Subesophageal Zone (SEZ).
source: These neurons are promising candidates to mediate postmating feeding changes because their processes descend into the prow region of the Subesophageal Zone (SEZ; Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), a brain region implicated in energy homeostasis and feeding (Shiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The prow region of the SEZ is a brain region implicated in energy homeostasis and feeding.
source: These neurons are promising candidates to mediate postmating feeding changes because their processes descend into the prow region of the Subesophageal Zone (SEZ; Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), a brain region implicated in energy homeostasis and feeding (Shiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Shiu et al., 2022.

claim: pC1 and SAG are cholinergic.
source: As pC1 and SAG are cholinergic (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020), pCd-2 cells likely receive excitatory signals from these two upstream synaptic partners and, therefore, would be predicted to be less active in mated females (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: pCd-2 cells likely receive excitatory signals from SAG and pC1 and would be predicted to be less active in mated females.
source: As pC1 and SAG are cholinergic (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020), pCd-2 cells likely receive excitatory signals from these two upstream synaptic partners and, therefore, would be predicted to be less active in mated females (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the cholinergic nature of upstream neurons.

claim: pCd-2a and pCd-2b neurons are female-specific.
source: We generated split-GAL4 lines to genetically access pCd-2a and pCd-2b (Figure 5E and F) and found that both neurons are female-specific (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with a role in female postmating behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of pC1 caused significant calcium increases in pCd-2a and pCd-2b neurons.
source: In both cases, neural activation caused significant calcium increases in pCd-2a and pCd-2b neurons (Figure 5G and H), validating pCd-2a and pCd-2b as targets of the mating status pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Optogenetically silencing pCd-2a or pCd-2b neurons in virgins significantly increased sucrose consumption compared to controls.
source: When we optogenetically silenced pCd-2a or pCd-2b neurons in virgins, mimicking the mated state (Figure 5D), females significantly increased sucrose consumption compared to controls (Figure 5I and J, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figures 5I and 5J.

claim: Silencing pCd-2a or pCd-2b did not influence egg laying.
source: Importantly, silencing pCd-2a or pCd-2b did not influence egg laying (Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B), demonstrating the separation of circuits for increased sucrose consumption from other behaviors downstream of pC1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Mated females with pCd-2a or pCd-2b silenced further increased sucrose consumption.
source: Instead, we found that mated females with pCd-2a or pCd-2b silenced further increased sucrose consumption (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), suggesting that optogenetic inhibition is stronger than mating-induced inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mated females with pCd-2a artificially activated significantly reduced sugar intake compared to controls.
source: We found that mated females with pCd-2a artificially activated significantly reduced sugar intake compared to controls, recapitulating the virgin phenotype in mated females (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mated females with pCd-2b artificially activated did not differ from controls.
source: However, mated females with pCd-2b artificially activated did not differ from controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), which may be a reflection of the fewer number of synapses from SAG and pC1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: pCd-2a and pCd-2b activity regulate sucrose consumption in virgin and mated females, with decreased activity promoting consumption after mating.
source: Thus, pCd-2a and pCd-2b activity regulate sucrose consumption in virgin and mated females, with decreased activity promoting consumption after mating.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the pCd-2 manipulation experiments.

claim: The major downstream targets of pCd-2 are t-shape cells (872 synapses).
source: To examine how pCd-2 neurons influence sucrose consumption, we used EM analyses and identified the major downstream targets of pCd-2 as t-shape cells (872 synapses) having processes in the SEZ prow region and a neuroendocrine center, the pars intercerebralis, with terminal arbors similar to insulin-producing cells and other median secretory cells (Liao and Nässel, 2020; Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by connectomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: T-shape cells have processes in the SEZ prow region and the pars intercerebralis.
source: To examine how pCd-2 neurons influence sucrose consumption, we used EM analyses and identified the major downstream targets of pCd-2 as t-shape cells (872 synapses) having processes in the SEZ prow region and a neuroendocrine center, the pars intercerebralis, with terminal arbors similar to insulin-producing cells and other median secretory cells (Liao and Nässel, 2020; Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: T-shape cells are leucine-rich repeat G-protein-coupled receptor-expressing medial bundle neurons (Lgr3 + mBNs).
source: Based on anatomical similarity, these cells are leucine-rich repeat G-protein-coupled receptor-expressing medial bundle neurons (Lgr3 + mBNs; Dolan et al., 2007; Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Dolan et al., 2007 and supported by anatomical data.

claim: Lgr3 expression is sexually dimorphic, with a greater number of cells in the central brain and abdominal ganglia of females.
source: Lgr3 expression is sexually dimorphic, with a greater number of cells in the central brain and abdominal ganglia of females (Meissner et al., 2016), consistent with a role in female behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Meissner et al., 2016.

claim: Lgr3 is a receptor for the Drosophila insulin-like peptide 8 (Dilp8).
source: Moreover, Lgr3 is a receptor for the Drosophila insulin-like peptide 8 (Dilp8; Colombani et al., 2015; Garelli et al., 2015; Vallejo et al., 2015), and both Lgr3 and Dilp8 are known to regulate feeding (Yeom et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Colombani et al., 2015; Garelli et al., 2015; Vallejo et al., 2015.

claim: Both Lgr3 and Dilp8 are known to regulate feeding.
source: Moreover, Lgr3 is a receptor for the Drosophila insulin-like peptide 8 (Dilp8; Colombani et al., 2015; Garelli et al., 2015; Vallejo et al., 2015), and both Lgr3 and Dilp8 are known to regulate feeding (Yeom et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Yeom et al., 2021.

claim: Optogenetic activation of pCd-2a or pCd-2b caused significant calcium decreases in Lgr3+ neurons.
source: In both cases, neural activation caused significant calcium decreases in Lgr3+ neurons (Figure 6D and E), validating Lgr3+ mBNs as targets of pCd-2 and the mating status pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Increased activity in Lgr3+ mBNs promotes sucrose consumption, mimicking the mated state.
source: We found that increased activity in Lgr3+ mBNs promotes sucrose consumption, mimicking the mated state (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Lgr3+ mBNs receive inputs from the canonical postmating circuit and are part of a neuroendocrine pathway that regulates sucrose consumption in postmated females.
source: Together, these studies reveal that Lgr3+ mBNs receive inputs from the canonical postmating circuit and are part of a neuroendocrine pathway that regulates sucrose consumption in postmated females.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the Lgr3+ mBN experiments.

claim: The mechanism that regulates postmating sugar intake is independent of the caloric deficiencies caused by egg production and is anticipatory in nature.
source: Although mated females are predicted to need more sugar to support increased reproductive output, we find that the mechanism that regulates postmating sugar intake is independent of the caloric deficiencies caused by egg production and is anticipatory in nature.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the eggless female experiments.

claim: The postmated increase in sugar feeding is due primarily to an elongation of feeding bouts rather than an increased likelihood of initiating a feeding event.
source: The postmated increase in sugar feeding is due primarily to an elongation of feeding bouts rather than an increased likelihood of initiating a feeding event or an increase in the appetitive nature of sugar.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the feeding microstructure data from Figure 1.

claim: There is no change in response of the sucrose-sensing gustatory sensory neurons across mating states.
source: This is supported by data that demonstrates no change in response of the sucrose-sensing gustatory sensory neurons across mating states.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the calcium imaging data from Figure 2.

claim: In virgins, elevated activity of SAG and pC1 potentiates pCd-2-mediated inhibition of Lgr3+ cells, resulting in low sugar intake.
source: In virgins, elevated activity of SAG and pC1 potentiates pCd-2-mediated inhibition of Lgr3+ cells, resulting in low sugar intake.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the circuit mechanism.

claim: After mating, the activity of SAG and pC1 is reduced, decreasing the activity of pCd-2 and alleviating the inhibition from Lgr3+ cells, increasing sucrose intake.
source: After mating, the activity of SAG and pC1 is reduced (Feng et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020), decreasing the activity of pCd-2 and alleviating the inhibition from Lgr3+ cells, increasing sucrose intake.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the circuit mechanism with citations.

claim: Expression levels of Lgr3 and Dilp8 rise in fed flies and mutations in either gene increase feeding.
source: Expression levels of Lgr3 and Dilp8 rise in fed flies and mutations in either gene increase feeding, arguing that Dilp8 and Lgr3 are satiety factors (Yeom et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Yeom et al., 2021.

claim: Dilp8 and Lgr3 are satiety factors.
source: Expression levels of Lgr3 and Dilp8 rise in fed flies and mutations in either gene increase feeding, arguing that Dilp8 and Lgr3 are satiety factors (Yeom et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Yeom et al., 2021.

claim: Lgr3+ mBN neurons are more active in a mated state.
source: Our calcium imaging and behavioral studies of Lgr3+ mBNs indicate that they are more active in a mated state and activation of these neurons promotes sucrose consumption.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental results.

claim: In virgin or satiated female flies, pCd-2 activity and circulating DILP8 inhibit Lgr3+ mBNs, reducing sugar feeding.
source: In virgin or satiated female flies, pCd-2 activity and circulating DILP8, respectively, inhibit Lgr3+ mBNs, reducing sugar feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed model shown in Figure 7.

claim: In mated or hungry flies, Lgr3+ mBNs lack the inhibitory signal from pCd-2 neurons or circulating Dilp8, resulting in increased sugar consumption.
source: Conversely, in mated or hungry flies, Lgr3+ mBNs lack the inhibitory signal from pCd-2 neurons or circulating Dilp8, respectively, resulting in increased sugar consumption.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed model shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mated state may be viewed mechanistically as an additional 'hunger' signal within this system.
source: Hence, the mated state may be viewed mechanistically as an additional 'hunger' signal within this system.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The three-tier mating status circuit (SPSN-SAG-pC1) regulates postmated changes in sucrose consumption.
source: Consistent with the neural regulation of other postmating behaviors, including other postmated changes in feeding, the three-tier mating status circuit (SPSN-SAG-pC1) regulates postmated changes in sucrose consumption.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the circuit manipulation experiments.

claim: The neural regulation of postmating sucrose consumption is regulated by an independent pathway postsynaptic to the mating status circuit.
source: Moreover, the neural regulation of postmating sucrose consumption, like other postmated behaviors, is also regulated by an independent pathway postsynaptic to the mating status circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the identification of pCd-2 neurons.

claim: The neural mechanisms regulating increased sugar intake and egg production are independent downstream of pC1.
source: Interestingly, although increased sugar intake may indeed support egg production, the neural mechanisms regulating the two behaviors are independent downstream of pC1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the finding that pCd-2 manipulation affects feeding but not egg laying.

claim: Mated-related changes in sucrose were not due to changes in sensory neuron sensitivity.
source: However, we found that mated-related changes in sucrose were not due to changes in sensory neuron sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the gustatory neuron imaging data from Figure 2.

claim: Mated-related changes in gustatory neuron sensitivity to yeast have not been found.
source: Similarly, mated-related changes in gustatory neuron sensitivity to yeast have not been found (Steck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Steck et al., 2018.

claim: After mating females display a transient modulation in chemosensory neurons that respond to polyamines.
source: It should be noted that after mating females display a transient modulation in chemosensory neurons that respond to polyamines (Hussain et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Hussain et al., 2016.

claim: Transient modulation in chemosensory neurons that respond to polyamines is not associated with polyamine consumption but instead oviposition behavior.
source: However, these changes are not associated with polyamine consumption but instead oviposition behavior (Hussain et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Hussain et al., 2016.

claim: Changes in postmated feeding behavior result from the mating status circuit modulating nutrient-sensing or feeding circuits, rather than directly tuning sensory neurons to promote feeding.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that changes in postmated feeding behavior result from the mating status circuit (or its output neurons) modulating nutrient-sensing or feeding circuits, rather than directly tuning sensory neurons to promote feeding.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: There is no shared circuit yet identified for elevated nutrient intake of sugar and yeast in mated females beyond the three-tier mating status circuit.
source: Although mating status impinges on circuits that either process nutrient-sensing signals or regulate feeding circuits, there is no shared circuit yet identified for elevated nutrient intake of sugar and yeast in mated females.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on comparison with other studies.

claim: No overlap between areas of the brain modulating postmated increases in protein and sugar consumption has been found beyond the three-tier mating status circuit.
source: Beyond the three-tier mating status circuit, no overlap between areas of the brain modulating postmated increases in protein (Liu et al., 2017; Münch et al., 2022) and sugar consumption (this manuscript) has been found.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to Liu et al., 2017; Münch et al., 2022.

claim: An elevated appetite for sucrose is an important behavioral subprogram elicited by mating and executed by female-specific circuitry.
source: Overall, our findings show that an elevated appetite for sucrose is an important behavioral subprogram elicited by mating and executed by female-specific circuitry, shifting the physiology of a mated female.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The activation of hunger centers by the mating status circuit provides a neural mechanism that anticipates the large energetic demands associated with offspring production and increases caloric intake, promoting reproductive success.
source: The activation of hunger centers by the mating status circuit provides a neural mechanism that anticipates the large energetic demands associated with offspring production and increases caloric intake, promoting reproductive success.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion about the biological significance of the findings.
